title: Who Gets to Vote
objective: After this level you can explain how the right to vote expanded over time.
summary: Suffrage, the right to vote, once needed property in Britain and was denied by race in places. US amendments and the UN Declaration widened it; Austria now votes at 16.

cards.headline: For a long time, voting wasn't a right. It came with property.
cards.body: In 18th- and 19th-century Britain, you needed property or a certain income to vote. The argument was that only people with "a stake in the country" should have a voice in its public affairs. So how did the vote get from the propertied few to the rest?

cards.headline: Suffrage: who's in, who's out
cards.body: Suffrage is the right to vote, in electing public officials and, where a country allows it, on proposed laws. Every country draws a line around who has it. Some lines were drawn by race: South Africa at one time, and the Old South of the United States, did not permit their Black populations to vote. This level follows that line as it moved.

events.label: 15th Amendment: no denying the vote on account of race, color or previous servitude
24th Amendment: no poll tax as a condition of voting in federal elections
26th Amendment: no denying the vote on account of age to citizens 18 or older

cards.headline: A world standard: universal and equal
cards.body: Level 34's Declaration set a benchmark in 1948. Article 21 says the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government, expressed in periodic and genuine elections by universal and equal suffrage, held by secret vote. Recall Level 3: authority is power people accept as legitimate. Article 21 names elections as the way that acceptance is expressed.

cards.fact: In 2007 Austria lowered its voting age from 18 to 16.
cards.context: Austria's parliament says it was the first country in Europe to lower the voting age to 16 for all citizens. From property owners to 16-year-olds: the line is still moving.

mascot.line: Property, race, age: each line on this card was once taken for granted.

cards.headline: Suffrage: expanded
learned: Suffrage is the right to vote
Britain once required property: a stake in the country
US amendments barred limits by race, poll tax and age

questions.prompt: What argument supported property qualifications for voting in 18th- and 19th-century Britain?

options.label: Elections were too expensive to run for everyone
options.rationale: The argument was about having a stake in the country.

options.label: Only those with a stake in the country should have a voice
Property owners were the only people who could read
options.rationale: The stated reason was a stake in the country.

options.label: The king wanted fewer elections to be held
options.rationale: The argument concerned who had a stake in the country.

questions.explanation: Voting required property or income, on the argument that only those with a stake in the country should have a voice in its affairs.

questions.prompt: What did the 26th Amendment, ratified in 1971, do?

options.label: Banned poll taxes in federal elections
Barred denying the vote on account of race
Lowered the voting age to 16 nationwide
Barred denying the vote to citizens 18 or older because of age

questions.explanation: The 26th Amendment says citizens who are 18 or older can't be denied the vote on account of age.

questions.prompt: Level 3 called authority accepted power. According to Article 21 of the Declaration, what should be the basis of a government's authority?

options.label: The wealth of the country's property owners
options.rationale: That was Britain's old voting rule, not Article 21.

options.label: The strength of the country's army
options.rationale: That's power, not the authority Article 21 describes.

options.label: The will of the people, expressed in genuine elections
Approval by the United Nations
options.rationale: Article 21 points to the people, not the UN.

questions.explanation: Article 21: the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government, expressed in periodic and genuine elections.
